title: Shape Is the Job
principle: What a protein does depends on the shape it is, not what it is made of.

t: Almost everything your body does is done by a protein. They are all made of the same twenty beads.
Muscle, sight, digestion, clotting, immunity, the machine that copies your DNA — all proteins, all built from the same twenty amino acids in different orders.
sub: So what makes one different from another?
Identical parts list, wildly different jobs. Only one thing can be carrying the difference.

question: If you changed a protein's shape but kept all the same beads, what would happen?
Denature a protein without breaking a single covalent bond. What happens to its function?
options: Nothing — it has the same parts
note: Commit. Everything in the protein is still present and still connected — only the arrangement has changed.

stages.label: Change the shape
captions: Slightly distorted. It still works, a bit slower.
Noticeably wrong. Most of the activity has gone.
Badly unfolded. It does nothing at all.
Completely open. Every bead still there, and useless.
t: Nothing is being removed. Only the shape is changing.
Not one bond is broken across this range. Watch how fast function falls away anyway.
after: Every bead is still there. It does nothing.
Composition unchanged from start to finish. Function is a property of the arrangement, not of the ingredients.

t: What a protein does depends on the shape it is, not what it is made of.
Function follows structure. The composition is nearly the same across every protein; the fold is what differs.
Structure determines function, and it does so through surface geometry: which residues are exposed, in what arrangement, forming what pockets.

This is why proteins are described as molecular machines rather than molecules. What matters is the shape of the surface and how it moves — the chemistry of the individual side chains is nearly the same set in all of them.
sub: Change the shape and you have changed the job.
A protein's shape IS its specification. Distort it and you have not damaged a working thing — you have made a different, useless thing.
Many proteins also change shape as part of working, and that motion is often the mechanism rather than an incidental.

Allostery makes the point sharply: binding at one site changes the shape at a distant one, so the molecule acts as a switch. Haemoglobin's cooperativity is exactly this, and it is why it can load oxygen in the lungs and release it in tissue.

q: You unfold a protein but break nothing. Does it still work?
An unfolded protein retains every bond. Is it functional?
Why does denaturation abolish function without altering composition?
options: No — the shape was the job
Yes, all the parts are still there
Only if it was a small protein
why: Nothing has been taken away. But the working part of a protein is the shape of its surface, and once that is gone there is nothing left to do the job.
Every atom and every covalent bond is intact. Function lived in the arrangement — the pocket, the surface, the geometry — and unfolding destroys that while leaving the chemistry untouched.

The catalytic or binding site is an emergent property of the tertiary structure: residues far apart in sequence are brought together in space to form it. Unfolding separates them, and the site simply ceases to exist as a feature.

t: Cooking an egg is exactly this. The clear part goes white and never goes back.

Egg white turning opaque is denaturation you can watch: heat unfolds the proteins, the exposed oily interiors stick to each other, and they aggregate. Nothing has been chemically destroyed — and it is irreversible for the same reason a tangled net is, because the aggregate is more stable than the folded form.
